You are a senior editor at Nature Communications.

Read the paper and the peer-review interaction below. Based on the scientific concerns raised by the reviewers and the authors' point-by-point response, predict the editorial outcome.

Respond with EXACTLY one of these labels on the first line:
  major_revision
  minor_revision
  accept

Then provide a 2–3 sentence rationale explaining your prediction.

## Paper

## Abstract

CD4⁺ T cells support the priming, expansion, and function of CD8⁺ T cells through dendritic cells. Precursor exhausted T cells (Tpex) maintain self-renewal and supply cytotoxic CD8⁺ T cells in the tumor
microenvironment (TME), but the identity of their CD4⁺ T-cell partners remains unclear. Here, we perform
scRNA-seq, scTCR-seq, and mass cytometry analysis on peripheral blood, tumor, and lymph nodes
primarily from lung cancer patients and, in part, renal cell carcinoma. We identify an IL-7Rhigh CCR6⁺ Th1-
like CD4⁺ T cell-population, named Th7R, that is numerically and spatially partnered with Tpex. Th7R
cells express lymphotoxin-β and CXCL13, correlate with high endothelial venules, and co-localize with
Tpex in tertiary lymphoid structures. Th7R cell abundance correlates with Tpex numbers in the TME and
lymph nodes, and adoptive transfer of Th7R increases Tpex in a preclinical mouse model. Intratumoral
Th7R and Tpex associate with improved response to neoadjuvant PD-1 blockade therapy. These results
suggest that Th7R cells act as partners of Tpex to sustain antitumor T-cell immunity.

---

## Introduction

Precursor-exhausted CD8+ T cells (Tpex) were first reported in a chronic viral infection model as
programmed cell death-1 (PD-1)-expressing exhausted T cells that also express CXCR5 and TCF7, possess
self-renewal capacity, and play a critical role in controlling persistent viral infections 1-3. Tpex function as
the starting point for the proliferation burst of CD8+ T cells induced by PD-1 blockade therapy 2. Single-
cell RNA sequencing of tumor tissue revealed that Tpex are a subset of stem-like memory T cells with self-
renewal capacity, sustaining long-term antitumor immunity in the tumor microenvironment (TME) while
providing GZMB+ exhausted CD8+ T cells4,5. Tpex infiltrate TME via high-endothelial venules (HEVs),
and localize within tertiary lymphoid structures (TLS) 6,7.
Ferris et al. reported that dendritic cells that have taken up tumor antigens first present these antigens
to CD4⁺ T cells. Dendritic cells that have been licensed through interaction with CD4⁺ T cells can then
induce the proliferation of CD8⁺ T cells 8. Primed CD8+ T cells also require antigen presentation from
dendritic cells licensed by CD4+ T cells to acquire cytotoxic function9. Thus, the helper function of CD4+
T cells is essential for the priming, proliferation, and induction of cytotoxic function in CD8+ T cells.
However, the role of CD4+ T cells in the generation and maintenance of Tpex has not been addressed.
Recently, it has been reported that CD8⁺ T cells exhausted by repeated antigen stimulation can undergo
epigenetic changes through the formation of a triad—a direct contact between CD4⁺ T cells, dendritic cells,
and CD8⁺ T cells—leading to the expression of IL-7 receptor (IL-7R) and TCF7, which are characteristic
of Tpex 10. Magen et al. reported that in TME of hepatocellular carcinoma that responded to preoperative
PD-1 blockade therapy, both CXCL13+ CD4+ T cells and GZMK+ CD8+ T cells clonally proliferated and
played crucial roles in antitumor immunity. They concluded that intratumoral niches containing CXCL13+
CD4+ T cells control the differentiation of tumor-specific progenitor exhausted CD8+ T cells through the
formation of triad with dendritic cells 11. CD4⁺ T cells are also involved in the formation of ectopic HEVs,
which are essential for Tpex to infiltrate the tumor microenvironment 12. Although CD4+ T cells seem to
play an important role in situation that require persistent immune responses, such as cancer, the specific
CD4⁺ T cell subset that assists Tpex remains poorly defined.
Upon priming, CD4⁺ T cells differentiate into functionally distinct subsets 13. While type1 helper T
cells (Th1) are traditionally linked with antitumor immunity through IFN-γ and T-bet expression, recent
analyses of immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) responses have identified Th1-like, non-canonical CD4⁺ T
cells in tumors. We previously described a unique CD4⁺ T-cell population, Th7R, which expresses TCF7
and IL-7R and is associated with better outcomes in lung cancer patients treated with ICIs or surgery 14,15.
Based on their shared molecular features with Tpex, such as IL-7R and TCF7 expression, we
hypothesize that Th7R cells may function as CD4⁺ T-cell partners of Tpex. In this study, we analyze TME
and peripheral blood using scRNA-seq, scTCR-seq, and imaging mass cytometry to define the relationship
between Th7R cells and Tpex in antitumor immunity. By identifying Th7R cells as key CD4⁺ T-cell partners
of Tpex, this study bridges fundamental T-cell differentiation biology with clinically relevant antitumor
immune dynamics. Our findings suggest that CD4⁺ T-cell–mediated support of Tpex represents a critical
axis governing durable responses to immune checkpoint blockade and tumor control. This conceptual
advance opens new avenues for patient stratification and for therapeutic strategies that selectively enhance
or restore CD4⁺–CD8⁺ T-cell cooperation in cancer.

---

## Results

Cells with the same TCR clonotypes and gene expression signature as Th7R cells in the peripheral
blood are present in the tumor microenvironment.
Th7R is a novel Th1-like CD4+ T-cell cluster identified by scRNA-seq analysis of peripheral blood
from advanced-stage lung cancer patients who responded to immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy 14.
To clarify whether Th7R cells are also present in the tumor microenvironment (TME), we analyzed the
scRNA-seq and scTCR-seq data of CD4+ T cells derived from the peripheral blood and tumor tissues of
eight stage Ⅰ-Ⅱ lung cancer patients (5 males, 3 females, aged 62-80 years) who had undergone surgery and
examined whether CD4+ T-cell clusters with the same gene expression patterns and TCR clonotypes as
peripheral blood Th7R cells are present in lung cancer tissues. A total of 79,130 CD4+CD3D+ cells (65,572
PB-CD3D+CD4+ cells and 13,558 TIL-CD3D+CD4+ cells) were subjected to unsupervised clustering on the
basis of 2,000 genes with highly variable expression, generating 27 clusters (Fig. 1a, Supplementary Table
1, 2, Supplementary Fig. 1 a, b). Since Th7R cells were discovered in a cluster of effector T cells with
low SELL expression in the peripheral blood, we first focused on the SELL low-expression clusters 13, 14,
18, 21, and 26 (Fig. 1b). The SELL low-expression clusters contained many clonally expanded T cells (Fig.
1c, Supplementary Table 3). Cluster 8 and 11, which contained many multicellular clonotypes with high
SELL expression in the TME, was thought to include regulatory T cells (Tregs) with high FoxP3 expression
(Fig. 1d).
The SELLlow effector CD4+T T cells in the peripheral blood included canonical Th1-type cells, Th17-
type cells and Th7R cells, and chemokine receptor expression patterns revealed that these cells were
CXCR3+ CCR4- CCR6- Th1 cells, CXCR3- CCR4+CCR6+ Th17 cells, and CXCR3± CCR4- CCR6+ Th7R
cells, respectively14. Next, we examined the signature genes that could discriminate among Th1, Th17, and
Th7R cells. First, CXCR3+ CCR4- CCR6-, CXCR3- CCR4+ CCR6+, and CXCR3± CCR4- CCR6+ T cells
sorted from the peripheral blood of CD62Llow CD4+ T cells from lung cancer patients (sorted Th cohort,
n=3) were analyzed by scRNA-seq (Supplementary Table 1). Differential expression analysis identified 64
genes that were differentially expressed among these subsets, including both upregulated and
downregulated genes, thereby enabling the characterization of gene expression signatures associated with
the Th1, Th7R, and Th17 phenotypes. (Supplementary Data 1). We refined the 64-gene set to 58 genes by
applying support vector machine-based recursive feature elimination (SVM-RFE) for feature selection
(Supplementary Fig. 2 a-c). By using the expression data for the 58 selected genes from sorted Th1, Th7R,
and Th17 cells, we trained an SVM classifier and applied it to discriminate the Th subtypes of the cell
clusters shown in Fig. 1a. As a result, cluster 13 and 26 were predicted to be Th1 cells, cluster 14 was
predicted to be Th17 cells, and cluster 18 and 21 were predicted to be Th7R cells (Supplementary Fig. 2 d,
e). We evaluated the similarity of the sorted subsets and SVM-predicted clusters using an expression
heatmap of 58 genes combined with cosine similarity analysis. This approach revealed strong concordance
indicating that the cluster 13+26 cluster was Th1 and that the cluster 18+21 was Th7R (Fig. 1e). Robustness
of this SVM-prediction was examined using scRNA-seq data obtained from other 34 lung cancer patients
other than the 8 surgery patients, a public dataset of 135 healthy Japanese, 3 renal cell cancer patients, and
a public dataset of 4 melanoma patients (Supplementary Table 1, Supplementary Fig. 3 a-o). In all cohorts,
the clusters of Th1-type, Th17-type, and Th7R-type gene signature were consistently found in SELLlow
region of UMAP and the cosine similarity and the prediction probabilities indicated good concordance with
sorted Th.
Next, the independence of the TIL-13, TIL-14, TIL-18, TIL-21 and TIL-26 clusters was examined by
analyzing TCR sharing in multicellular TCR clonotypes, which included 2 or more T cells in each TIL
cluster (Fig. 1f). Among the Th1-type clusters, only TIL-13 contained multicellular clonotypes. The TIL-
13 clonotypes were only shared with the peripheral blood (PB)-13 cluster, indicating that the T cells
belonging to PB-13 do not significantly change their gene expression patterns even after infiltration into
the TME. TCR sharing with TIL-21 cells was found not only for the PB-21 cluster but also for the TIL-18
cluster. On the other hand, the clonotypes belonging to TIL-18 were mostly found in the PB-18 cluster.
Thus, T cells in the PB-21 cluster are likely to change their gene expression patterns to the cluster 18 state
after infiltrating the TME, suggesting that clusters 18 and 21 exhibit two gene expression states of one type
of differentiated T cell. Accordingly, clusters 18 and 21 were considered two closely related transcriptional
states of the same Th7R subset. TCR clonotypes belonging to the TIL-14 cluster were rarely detected in
other clusters. The total cell counts and TCR clone sizes for each cluster are shown in Fig. 1g. Cluster13
had greatly expanded TCR clones in the peripheral blood but lacked expanded TCR clones in the TME. It
is likely that the abundant multicellular clonotypes in the PB-13 cluster reflect clonal expansion in the
secondary lymphoid organs and that some of the expanded cells infiltrate the TME. In contrast, cluster 18
exhibited few expanded TCR clonotypes in the peripheral blood but the greatest number of expanded TCR
clonotypes in the TIL-18 cluster, suggesting clonal expansion in the TME rather than in the secondary
lymphoid organs.
Furthermore, to investigate whether this gene expression pattern is derived from epigenetic changes,
we used the 10x Genomics Multiome platform to perform both single-nucleus RNA-seq (snRNA-seq) and
single-cell ATAC-seq (scATAC-seq) of the same nuclei (Fig. 1h, Supplementary Fig. 4a). Among the
clusters obtained on the WNN-UMAP diagram, clusters 4, 6, 11, 14, and 20 were considered SELL low-
expression clusters (Supplementary Fig. 4b, c). On the basis of SVM-based prediction of Th subtypes using
the 58 signature genes, clusters 6 and 20 were classified as Th1 cells, cluster 14 was classified as Th17 cells,
and clusters 4 and 11 were classified as Th7R cells (Fig.1i, Supplementary Fig. 4d-f). The overall gene
expression patterns of the clusters classified as Th1, Th17, and Th7R cells were very similar to those of
sorted Th cells (Fig. 1j). The gene activity (GA) scores of 54 of the 58 signature genes obtained from DNA
chromatin information also matched the gene expression patterns of each Th subset (Fig. 1k). These results
indicate that Th7R cells have a characteristic gene expression pattern that differs from those of Th1 and
Th17 cells and that they have a DNA chromatin state that supports this gene expression profile.
Th7R cell gene expression in the TME
The SVM classifier was applied to the SELLlow clusters of TIL and PB to evaluate prediction
probabilities (Supplementary Fig. 5a). For #13+26 Th1 and #14 Th17 clusters, the peripheral blood
(prediction probability of 1.000, 1.000) and the TIL (0.999, 0.842), showed good predictive agreement. In
contrast, the #18+21 Th7R cluster had a greater probability in the peripheral blood (0.993) but a lower
probability in TILs (0.557), suggesting altered gene expression in the TME. However, the prediction
probability of the TIL Th7R cluster being classified as Th1 (0.171) or Th17 (0.272) was low, suggesting
that Th7R cells have a unique gene expression pattern in the TME. Therefore, we compared the gene
expression profile of the Th7R cluster between peripheral blood and TILs and found that 115 genes were
upregulated more than 2-fold in TILs and 18 genes were downregulated more than 2-fold in TILs (Fig. 2a,
b, Supplementary Data 2, Supplementary Fig. 5b). The genes upregulated in the TME included CCL4,
CXCL13, CREM, CCL4L2, GZMB, CTLA4, CXCR4, IFNG, ID2, XCL1, CXCR6, CCL3 and ICOS. Next,
we investigated the differences in gene expression between Th7R and Th1 or Th17 cells in the TME (Fig.
2c, Supplementary Fig. 5c). The genes whose expression was more than 2-fold greater in Th7R cells than
in canonical Th1 cells in the TME included LTB, CXCR6, CTLA4, and CXCL13 (Fig. 2d, Supplementary
Data 3). The genes whose expression was more than 2-fold greater in Th7R cells than in Th17 cells
included CCL4, CCL4L2, CXCL13, CCL5, GZMK, GZMB, IFNG, and CCL3.
Relationship between Th7R cells and HEV formation in the TME
CXCL13 was found to be upregulated in Th7R cells in the TME, with a significant difference from the
expression observed in Th1 and Th17 cells. Th7R cells also expressed more LTB; LTβ and CXCL13 are
known to be essential for the formation of ectopic HEVs and TLSs 16. To investigate the relationship
between Th7R cells and ectopic HEV formation, immunohistochemical (IHC) analysis and Hyperion
analysis were performed (n=56, Supplementary Table 1). Sections were stained with antibodies against the
normal vascular marker CD31 and the HEV marker peripheral node addressin (PNAd), and the ratio of
PNAd-positive areas to CD31-positive areas (the MECA index) was calculated to assess HEV density and
its relationship with the proportion of Th7R cells in the peripheral blood (Fig. 3a). The threshold of the
MECA index was determined using the value that yielded the highest likelihood ratio in ROC analysis for
distinguishing recurrent patients from non-recurrent patients. Consistent with previous reports, significantly
better disease-free survival (DFS) was observed in patients with more HEV formation in the TME, and a
MECA index of 0.044 was found to predict better DFS (Fig. 3b). A chi-square test using a Th7R percentage
of 3.05, which was used as a threshold for predicting better DFS after surgery for lung cancer in a previous
study, and a MECA index of 0.044 showed that HEV density was associated with Th7R abundance (P =
0.0080, Fig. 3c) 15.
Tpex as a source of Tex in the TME
Tpex have self-renewal ability and contribute to a sustained supply of CD8+ T cells to maintain long-
term antitumor immunity through stem cell-like asymmetric cell division 7. To analyze the relationship
between Th7R cells and Tpex in the TME, we attempted to identify Tpex in lung cancer tissues. We
performed scRNA-seq analysis of 25,728 CD3D+CD8+ cells (17,997 PB-CD3D+CD8+ cells and 7,731 TIL-
CD3D+CD8+ cells) derived from 8 surgery patients. Unsupervised clustering was performed on the basis of
the expression of 2,000 highly variable genes, generating 16 clusters, as shown in the UMAP plot (Fig. 4a,
Supplementary Fig. 6a, b). We analyzed the gene expression of GZMK and GZMB as candidate markers
for discriminating among Tpex, exhausted CD8+ T cells (Tex), and unexhausted cytotoxic T lymphocytes
(CTLs) (Fig. 4b) 4,5,17. GZMK expression was observed in clusters 1, 2, 4, 8, 10, 11, 13 and 14 adjacent to
the SELLhighCD45RA+ naive clusters (6, and 15) and the SELLhighCD45RA- central memory (CM) cluster
(3, 7, and 12) (Fig. 4c, Supplementary Fig. 6c). GZMB expression was observed in cluster 5, which was
farthest from the naive clusters, and clusters 1, 4, 8, 11, and 13. Cluster 9 was CCR6+ and was considered
mucosa-associated invariant T (MAIT) cells. Next, we assessed the expression of signature genes thought
to characterize Tpex in each TIL cluster (Fig. 4d) 7. GZMK+GZMB- clusters 2, 10, and 14
expressed TCF7, IL-7R, PDCD1, SELL, and CCR7, matching the characteristics for Tpex. Tpex is known
to undergo asymmetric division, containing a population that remains in a more stem-like state and a
population acquiring effector functions 5. Although the GZMK+GZMB- cluster comprises multiple sub-
clusters, the entire cluster will be referred to as GZMK+GZMB- Tpex in this study. On the other hand,
GZMK-GZMB+ cluster 5 was considered a CTL cluster because it expressed no exhaustion genes and highly
expressed PRF1, GZMB, GNLY, FGFBP2, and NKG7. The GZMK+GZMB+ clusters 1, 4, 8, 11, and 13
were considered Tex, as they did not express IL-7R or TCF7 but highly expressed exhaustion genes such
as PDCD1, CTLA-4, ENTPD1, and HAVCR2. These results indicate that Tpex, Tex, and CTLs can be
distinguished on the basis of their GZMB and GZMK expression patterns.
When the cell density of each pixel in the PB-UMAP plot was subtracted from the cell density of each
pixel in the TIL-UMAP plot, clusters 1, 2, 10 and 13 presented a distribution with a TME-dominance (Fig.
4e, Supplementary Table 4). The direction of the state change for each cluster in the TME and peripheral
blood was also examined by velocity analysis (Fig. 4f). In the peripheral blood, changes to the Tex clusters
starting from cluster 5, which is a cluster of CTLs that have not been exhausted, were observed, and it was
thought that CTLs that proliferated in the secondary lymphoid organs changed their state in response to
repeated antigen stimulation. In contrast, TIL velocity analysis revealed that cluster 2, which was included
in GZMK+GZMB- Tpex, was the source of the surrounding clusters, including Tex. Considering that
clusters 1 and 2 were dominant in the TME, the main progression of T-cell state changes is thought to be
from the GZMK+GZMB- Tpex cluster 2 to the terminally exhausted cluster 1, which has the highest
expression of HAVCR2, CTLA4, and ENTPD1. TIL-1 and 2 are the clusters containing the highest number
of clonally expanded cells in TME. The fact that many TCR clonotypes belonging to the TIL-2 cluster were
shared with TIL-1 suggests that the cells in TIL-2 is transformed into the TIL-1 phenotype (Supplementary
Fig. 6d, e). These results indicate that Tex, which have cytotoxic activity, are supplied mainly by Tpex,
which replicate in the TME.
Spatial relationship between Th7R cells and GZMK+GZMB- Tpex in TLSs
IHC analysis revealed that CXCR3+CCR6+ CD4+ T cells were located in TLSs (Supplementary Fig.
7). Next, we performed a neighborhood analysis of Th7R cells and GZMK+GZMB- Tpex on the basis of
the molecular expression information obtained using Hyperion (Fig. 5a). We used software that can segment
and annotate individual cells on the basis of their molecular expression patterns (Fig. 5b, Supplementary
Fig. 8). GZMB+ cells, which constitute a population with cytolytic functions, were found in the cancer cell
nest. In contrast, GZMB-GZMKT+ CD8+ T cells, which are considered Tpex, were found to be abundant
within the B-cell aggregates considered TLSs. CXCR3+ CCR6+ CD4+ T cells, which are considered Th7R
cells, were found near GZMK+GZMB- Tpex within TLSs (Fig. 5c).
Correlations between Th7R and GZMK+GZMB- Tpex numbers
Next, we examined whether the percentages of CTLs and GZMK+GZMB- Tpex among total CD8+ T
cells were correlated with the percentages of Th1 and Th7R cells among total CD4+ T cells in cluster 12 in
the draining lymph nodes (the hilar lymph nodes) and peripheral blood derived from lung cancer patients
(Fig. 6a, b). In both locations, Th1 cell abundance was positively correlated with CTL abundance, and Th7R
abundance was positively correlated with GZMK+GZMB- Tpex abundance. To eliminate overlapping
relationships and clarify the relationships between cells, a quantitative network analysis of the proportions
of clusters in CD4+ T cells and CD8+ T cells relative to CD3+ cells in the peripheral blood was performed
(Fig. 6c). Notably, the only CD4+ T-cell cluster whose abundance directly correlated with that of
GZMK+GZMB- Tpex was Th7R cells, with a connection established in 1000 out of 1000 interferences.
These results support the hypothesis that Th7R cells are involved in the intratumoral infiltration and
proliferation of Tpex.
Th7R cell therapy in a mouse tumor model
To determine whether increased Th7R abundance in the TME affects CD8+ T-cell counts, we analyzed
TILs from mice subjected to adoptive transfer of Th7R cells. Th7R cells were sorted as CXCR3±CCR4-
CCR6+ CD4+ T cells and Th1 as CXCR3+CCR4-CCR6- CD4+ T cells from inguinal lymph nodes draining
a methylcholanthrene-induced fibrosarcoma MCA205 skin tumor, and after ex vivo culture, they were
adoptively transferred into mice bearing MCA205 skin tumors. Four million of Th1 or Th7R exhibited
antitumor therapeutic efficacy against 8-day tumors (Fig. 7a). The antitumor reactivity of Th7R is likely
tumor-antigen specific, since antitumor therapeutic efficacy was not observed in Th7R derived from LNs
draining B16 melanoma (Fig. 7b). To obtain TIL, seven days after tumor implantation, mice received
adoptive transfer of Th1 or Th7R cells. Six days post-transfer, tumors were harvested from four mice per
group for TIL isolation. TILs were dissociated with Liberase TL, enriched by Percoll density-gradient
centrifugation, and analyzed by mass cytometry. Both Th1 and Th7R transfer increased intratumoral CD8⁺
T-cell numbers. Notably, only Th7R transfer significantly expanded Tpex (PD-1⁺IL-7R⁺ CD8⁺ or PD-
1⁺TCF-1⁺ CD8⁺) and Tex (PD-1⁺TIM-3⁺ CD8⁺) populations (Fig. 7c, d). In the Th1 group, these populations
showed an upward trend that did not reach statistical significance, whereas CTL (PD-1⁻GZMB⁺ CD8⁺)
tended to increase. Therefore, Th7R cells likely promote asymmetric cell division of Tpex, resulting in
increases in Tpex as abundance and the supply of Tex. The effect of increased Tpex in the tumor
microenvironment induced by Th7R adoptive transfer was not observed in Th7R derived from LNs draining
B16 melanoma but was only observed in Th7R derived from LNs draining MCA205. This suggests the
effect occurs in an antigen-specific manner (Supplementary Fig. 9a, b).
Clinical significance of Th7R and Tpex
To evaluate whether Th7R contribute to antitumor immunity, we investigated their associations with
disease free progression (DFS) after surgery (n = 55, Supplementary Table 1) 18. In stage I-II lung cancer
patients with an observation period of 5 years or more, the patients with preoperative peripheral blood Th7R
≥ 3.05% demonstrated favorable DFS with a hazard ratio of 0.121 (95% CI 0.0306-0.479), P = 0.0002 (Fig.
8a). This Th7R threshold value was obtained in previous studies15. In contrast, preoperative Th1 levels
could not distinguish cases with favorable DFS. Furthermore, only Th7R significantly decreased after
resection of lung cancer tissues, while Th1 and Th17 remained unchanged (Fig. 8b). These results suggest
that Th7R numbers are driven by cancer antigens. Next, to evaluate whether Th7R cells and Tpex in the
TME contribute to antitumor immunity, we investigated their associations with those responses to
preoperative neoadjuvant therapy including anti-PD-1 antibody (n = 20, Supplementary Table 1) 18. There
was a significantly greater abundance of Tpex in the patients who achieved a RECIST partial response by
imaging. In addition, Th7R abundance was significantly greater in patients who achieved a complete
pathological response or major pathological response (Fig. 8c). Thus, Th7R cells and Tpex in the TME
likely play important roles as partners in antitumor immunity.

## Methods

Patients
TIL and peripheral blood samples for single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq, n = 8), along with
tissue samples for IHC analysis (n = 56, Supplementary Table 1) and Hyperion analysis, were collected
from patients with stage I–II non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) who underwent radical surgery between
October 2017 and October 2019 at Saitama Medical University International Medical Center (Hidaka city,
Saitama pref., Japan).
TIL samples for mass cytometry analysis were collected from patients (n = 20, Supplementary Table
1) with stage II-IIIA NSCLC who underwent surgery after 3 courses of neoadjuvant therapy, including
nivolumab and chemotherapy, between August 2023 and October 2024 at Saitama Medical University
International Medical Center. The response to treatment was assessed using Response Evaluation Criteria
in Solid Tumors (RECIST), version 1.1. Pathological response was independently assessed by pathologists.
All the samples were collected after written informed consent was obtained from the patients. The
Internal Review Board of Saitama Medical University International Medical Center approved the study
protocol, in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki (ethical approval Nos. 17-084, 15-221, and 2023-
011).
Blood samples
Peripheral blood samples were collected using heparinized CPT Vacutainer tubes (Becton Dickinson
Vacutainer Systems, Franklin Lakes, NJ, USA), as previously described27. The samples were preserved
using Cellbanker2 (Nippon Zenyaku Kogyo Co., Koriyama, Japan) in a liquid nitrogen tank. For T-cell
subset analyses, the cells were incubated for 32–48 h in RPMI 1640 medium supplemented with 10% fetal
calf serum (FCS) in a 5% CO incubator at 37 °C.
2
TIL samples
To extract TILs, the collected tumors were sectioned into 2–3-mm pieces and incubated with
Dulbecco's modified Eagle’s medium supplemented with Dri Tissue & Tumor Dissociation Reagent (BD
horizon: 661563; BD Biosciences, Franklin Lakes, NJ, USA) or with RPMI 1640 medium supplemented
with Liberase TL Research Grade (05401020001; Roche, Basel, Switzerland) following the manufacturer’s
instructions. Erythrocytes were removed using a biotin anti-human CD235ab antibody (306617; BioLegend,
San Diego, CA, USA) and streptavidin nanobeads (480016; BioLegend, San Diego, CA, USA) according
to the manufacturer’s instructions. Tissue dissociation and cell preparation were initiated immediately after
surgical resection, and the procedure was advanced to the point where processing could be safely paused
within the same day.
Multiplex immunohistochemical staining, and imaging mass cytometry image acquisition and data
analysis for tissue samples
The tumor samples were formalin fixed and paraffin embedded (FFPE), and the three tumors with the
largest areas of viable tumor cells were selected (Supplementary Table 1). Five-micron-thick sections were
deparaffinized and rehydrated with xylene and ethanol for multiplex immunohistochemical staining. All
the slides were sequentially treated with 0.3% hydrogen peroxide in methanol for 30 min to block
endogenous peroxidase activity. To expose the antigens, the sections were autoclaved in 10 mM sodium
citrate buffer (pH 6.0) for 20 min, heated in a microwave at 98 °C for 15 min, and then cooled for 30 min.
After rinsing in 0.05 M Tris-buffered saline containing 0.1% Tween 20, the sections were incubated
with various antibodies: mouse monoclonal CD4 (Leica Biosystems, clone 4B12, 1:300, high pH, retrieval),
mouse monoclonal CD8 (DAKO, clone C8/144B, 1:150, high pH, retrieval), mouse monoclonal CD31
(DAKO, clone JC70A, 1:400, pH 6, retrieval), rabbit monoclonal CCR6 (Abcam, clone EPR22259, 1:1000,
high pH, retrieval), rat monoclonal peripheral node addressin (Novus, clone MECA79, 1:200, pH 6,
retrieval), mouse monoclonal CXCR3 (BioLegend, clone G025H7, 1:300, pH 6, retrieval), CD20 (Akoya,
clone L26, 1:200, high pH, retrieval), and mouse monoclonal pan cytokeratin (Abcam, clone AE1/AE3,
1:100, pH 6, retrieval). All the slides were stained using an OPAL 7-color IHC kit (Akoya Biosciences
NEL811001KT, MA, USA). Immunofluorescence analysis was performed on the Mantra imaging platform
(Akoya Biosciences) using Mantra Snap software. Color separation was conducted with inForm Software
v2.5.1 (Akoya Biosciences, MAT) to extract image data. Multiplex immunohistochemical staining and data
analysis were performed according to previously described procedures28.
After heat-induced epitope retrieval, the tumor samples were subjected to Hyperion analysis. The
sections were incubated with conjugated monoclonal antibodies overnight at 4 °C (Supplementary Table
5). Following antibody incubation and washing, selected regions of interest (ROIs) were ablated with a
laser at a resolution of 1 µm, and the vaporized particles were analyzed. The acquired data were visualized
and analyzed using MCD Viewer and MCD Smart Viewer software (Standard BioTools). Pseudo-colored
composite images were generated for each marker to assess tissue morphology and marker expression
patterns. All images were reviewed at high resolution, and representative ROIs were selected for figure
preparation.
Cell sorting for scRNA-seq and scTCR-seq
For peripheral blood scRNA-seq analyses, CD3+ T cells were isolated from frozen PBMCs that had
been incubated for 36 hrs in CM with 5% CO at 37 °C, using Dynabeads Untouched Human T Cells
2
(11344D; Invitrogen). For TIL scRNA-seq analysis, samples were used after erythrocyte removal. For
scRNA-seq analysis of sorted Th cohort, CD4+ T cells were isolated as follows. CD62Llow CD4+ cells were
separated from cultured frozen PBMCs using Dynabeads. Untouched Human CD4 T Cells (11346D;
Invitrogen) and Human CD62L MicroBeads (130-091-758; Miltenyi Biotec, Bergisch Gladbach, Germany)
were used. For sorting, CD62LlowCD4+ T cells were stained for 30 min at room temperature with CXCR3
(353715, 353716; BioLegend), CCR4 (353429, 353430; BioLegend), and CCR6 (359410; BioLegend)
antibodies, each diluted 1:40, and subsequently using a Cell Sorter SH800Z (Sony Imaging Products &
Solutions Inc., Tokyo, Japan) prior to single-cell library construction (Supplementary Fig. 10a).
Library construction and sequencing for scRNA-seq and scTCR-seq of surgery cohort and sorted Th
cohort
All single-cell RNA-seq and scTCR-seq libraries were constructed using the Chromium controller and
Chromium Single-Cell Immune Profiling v2 kit (10x Genomics Inc., Pleasanton, CA, USA) to analyze gene
expression differences and T-cell receptor (TCR) repertoires among T-cell subpopulations. Several
TotalSeq-C antibody types (BioLegend Inc., San Diego, CA, USA) were used as feature barcodes to
separate T-cell subpopulations (Supplementary Table 6). All the libraries were constructed according to the
manufacturers’ standard protocols. The quality and quantity of the libraries were evaluated using a
Bioanalyzer High-Sensitivity Kit (Agilent Technologies, CA, USA). All libraries were sequenced on
DNBSEQ-G400 sequencers (MGI, Shenzhen, China) in paired-end mode (read 1:28 bp; read 2:90 bp)
according to the manufacturer’s standard protocol. The sequencing depth was targeted at 50,000 reads/cell
for gene expression libraries and 10,000 reads/cell for feature barcoding and TCR libraries. Details of the
libraries and sequence results are summarized in Supplementary Data 4.
Data preprocessing and quality control for scRNA-seq and scTCR-seq of surgery cohort and sorted
Th cohort
The sequenced reads were processed using Cell Ranger 6 and 7 software (10x Genomics Inc.,
Pleasanton, CA, USA) with the GRCh38 reference dataset (version 2020-A for gene expression and 5.0.0
(samples from surgery cohort) or 7.1.0 (sorted Th cohort) for the TCR repertoire) obtained from 10x
Genomics. This processing generated the gene expression/feature barcode (TotalSeq-C) unique molecular
identifier (UMI) count matrix and TCR repertoire data. Quality control, statistical analysis, and graphical
representation were performed using the Loupe browser (10x Genomics, Inc.) and the Seurat 5.2.1 package
in R software (version 4.4.1) (https://satijalab.org/seurat/)29,30. The gene expression library and feature
barcoding library from the same sample were processed simultaneously using the ‘cellranger count’
command. TCR libraries were processed using the ‘cellranger vdj’ command for each sample. TCR
repertoires from different samples (i.e., TILs and PBMCs) from the same patient were aggregated using the
‘cellranger aggr’ command to identify shared clonotypes across different libraries. Quality control of the
scRNA-seq data was executed as follows. cells with a valid TCR clonotype within the CD3D+ cluster were
selected using the Loupe browser. Genes expressed in fewer than three cells were excluded from the
analysis. Cells with either too few (≤200) or too many (>2,500-3000) expressed genes were excluded to
remove empty or multiple GEMs. Cells with a high percentage of mitochondrial genes (≥5–8%) were also
excluded to eliminate dead cells, and those with excessively high TotalSeq-C counts were removed to
minimize the impact of aggregated antibodies. These cutoff thresholds were set on the basis of the tail of
the distribution. Prior to analysis, the UMI gene expression counts were log-normalized using Seurat's
‘LogNormalize’ function (scale factor = 10,000).
scRNA-seq and scTCR-seq data integration and analysis of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells derived from
surgery cohort
The filtered CD3D+ T cells derived from surgical patients were categorized into CD4+CD3D+ T cells
and CD8+CD3D+ T cells on the basis of the RNA and surface protein expression of CD4 and CD8A prior
to integration (Supplementary Fig. 10b). CD3D⁺ T cells were annotated as CD4⁺ or CD8⁺ at the clonotype
level based on CD4 and CD8A expression in both RNA and surface protein data. For each clonotype, the
total number of CD4⁺ and CD8A⁺ cells (RNA⁺ + protein⁺) was compared, and the clonotype was assigned
according to the predominant signal, using a simple rule-based approach to handle variability across
modalities. The integration of these CD4+ and CD8+ T cells was conducted following the standard
integration workflow of Seurat version 5, utilizing the reciprocal PCA integration method. Initially, 2,000
highly variable genes (excluding TCR-related genes) were identified using the 'FindVariableFeatures'
function with the vst method. The expression of these variable genes was then scaled and centered using
the 'ScaleData' function. Principal component analysis was performed using the 'RunPCA' function,
followed by batch correction among samples using the reciprocal PCA method with the 'IntegrateLayers'
function. Unsupervised clustering of the integrated gene expression matrix was carried out using the
'FindNeighbors' (with the parameter “dims=1:30”) and 'FindClusters' functions of Seurat on the basis of the
shared nearest neighbor modularity optimization clustering algorithm31. The resolution parameter of
'FindClusters' was optimized on the basis of the number of expected clusters and the stability of the
clustering results. Visualization via a UMAP plot was performed with the 'RunUMAP' function.
Differential expression analysis was conducted using the MAST package in R software 32, implemented in the
'FindMarkers' function of the Seurat package. Genes with an adjusted P value < 0.05 and log -fold change
2
> 1 were considered significant and are indicated by red dots on volcano plots drawn with the
EnhancedVolcano package in R33. The RNA velocity was estimated using the velocyto 0.17.17 package
and scVelo 0.2.5 in Python 3.634. The Loom file with UMAP embedding calculated via Seurat analysis was
merged with the Loom file containing RNA velocity data from velocyto, and merged data were filtered and
normalized using the 'scvelo.pp.filter_and_normalize' function (min_shared_counts=5, n_top_genes=2000).
First- and second-order moments were computed for each cell across its nearest neighbors using the
'scvelo.pp.moments' function (n_pcs=30, n_neighbors=100). Finally, RNA velocities were estimated in the
dynamic model using the 'scvelo.tl.recover_dynamics' and 'scvelo.tl.velocity' functions. The estimated
velocity was visualized as a stream plot using the 'scvelo.pl.velocity_embedding_stream' function.
scRNA-seq analysis of sorted Th cohort
Preparation and quality control of scRNA-seq libraries from CD4+ T cells from sorted Th cohort were
performed in a manner similar to that used for PBMCs from surgical specimens, except that feature
barcoding technology with TotalSeq was not utilized. For cells that passed quality control, log-normalized
count data were merged for each patient, and differential expression gene analysis was conducted among
the four cell types, Th1, Th17, CXCR3+ Th7R, and CXCR3- Th7R, on a round-robin basis using the
‘FindMarkers’ function with the MAST method. This statistical test was applied to genes that were
expressed in more than 10% of the cells and exhibited a minimum log -fold change of 0.25. Genes with an
2
adjusted P value < 0.05 were considered differentially expressed. The 64 DEGs common to all three patients
were selected as candidate signature genes (Supplementary Data 1).
To identify CD4 signature genes and construct a predictive model for CD4 cell subtypes, we employed
support vector machines (SVMs). To mitigate the influence of variability in RNA expression at the single-
cell level, we created mini-clusters by averaging the gene expression profiles of 10 randomly sampled cells.
For each sorted population—Th1, Th7R, and Th17—we generated 4,000 mini-clusters and used them for
downstream analysis.
Feature selection was conducted using the 'rfeControl' function in the caret R package in combination
with a radial kernel SVM implemented using the e1071 package. On the basis of this feature selection
process, 58 genes were selected as relevant markers for classification.
By using the expression profiles of these 58 genes, we built an SVM-based classifier to distinguish
among the Th1, Th7R, and Th17 CD4 subtypes. Of the 4,000 mini-clusters generated per subtype, 2,000
were used for training, and the remaining 2,000 were used for testing to evaluate the model’s predictive
performance.
To annotate SELL low-expression clusters, the classifier was trained on all 12,000 mini-clusters (4,000
per subtype) generated from the sorted reference samples.
scRNA-seq analysis of PBMC samples from scRNA-seq cohort 2
PBMC samples were collected prior to treatment from 34 patients with lung cancer. scRNA-seq
libraries were generated using the Chromium Single Cell 5′ Gene Expression platform (10x Genomics).
Due to differences in sample collection time points, two versions of the chemistry were employed:
Chromium Single-Cell Immune Profiling v1.1 and v2 kits. Libraries were constructed and sequenced
according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Sequence data were processed using the Cell Ranger pipeline
(10x Genomics, versions 4.0.0 to 7.1.1) with default settings. Data preprocessing and quality control were
performed using the same workflow as for the other cohorts. Potential batch effects arising from differences
in kit chemistry and Cell Ranger versions were corrected using the standard Seurat integration workflow
described above. A summary of the sequencing results is summarized in Supplementary Data 5.
scRNA-seq analysis of PBMC from healthy Japanese donors derived from public database
To further validate our findings in an independent dataset, we utilized publicly available scRNA-seq
data from the Human Cell Atlas project (https://www.humancellatlas.org/), the Asian Immune Diversity
Atlas (AIDA) 35. We downloaded the AIDA Phase 1 Data Freeze v2 dataset in h5ad format from the
CELLxGENE portal (https://cellxgene.cziscience.com/collections/ced320a1-29f3-47c1-a735-
513c7084d508). Given the large size of the dataset, we restricted our analysis to samples collected in Japan
from self-reported Japanese donors (134 donors). Based on the author-provided annotations, we extracted
84,065 cells classified as CD4+_T, CD4+_T_CM, CD4+_T_cyt, CD4+_T_EM, CD4+_T_naive, and Treg.
Ensembl gene identifiers were converted to HGNC gene symbols (gene_name field) using the Annotation
Hub package (3.14.0) with EnsDb.Hsapiens.v98. The processed raw UMI count data were then imported
into Seurat and analyzed using the standard integration workflow as applied to our other cohorts, ensuring
methodological consistency.
scRNA-seq analysis of PBMC samples from 3 renal cancer patients
Preparation and quality control of scRNA-seq libraries from CD4+ T cells from 3 renal cancer patients were
performed in a manner similar to that used for PBMCs from surgical specimens, except that we applied the
CCA-based integration method in Seurat because the sample number was limited, whereas RPCA was used
for surgical datasets with larger sample sizes. A summary of the sequencing results is summarized in
Supplementary Data 5.
scRNA-seq analysis of PBMC samples from melanoma patients
PBMC-derived CD4 T-cell samples from melanoma patients were obtained by downloading scRNA-seq
count data and scTCR-seq data from four pretreatment (day 0) cases (p134, p145, p196 and p326) in the
NCBI GEO dataset GSE307261 36. Cells with excessively high nFeature_RNA values (> 2,000-2,500) and
excessively high percentage of mitochondrial genes (> 5-8 %) and those lacking valid TCR information
were excluded. The four samples were then integrated and analyzed following the same workflow used for
CD4 T-cell samples from surgical cases.
Single-nucleus multiomic profiling of gene expression and chromatin accessibility analysis
After a two-day culture of thawed frozen cells, CD4 staining was performed, and CD4+ cells were
sorted using a SH800Z cell sorter (Sony). Nuclei were extracted according to the 10x Genomics protocol
(CG000365, Rev C). The nuclear density was assessed by microscopy using the BZ-X700 system
(Keyence). All multiome libraries were constructed using the Chromium controller and Chromium Single
Cell Multiome ATAC + Gene Expression Kit (10x Genomics, Inc.) following the 10x Genomics protocol
(CG000338, Rev F). All multiome libraries were sequenced on DNBSEQ-G400 sequencers (MGI)
according to the manufacturer’s standard protocol.
The sequenced reads were processed using Cell Ranger ARC 2.0.2 software (10x Genomics, Inc.) with
the GRCh38 reference dataset (version 2020-A-2.0.0) obtained from 10x Genomics. Quality control,
statistical analysis, and graphical representation were performed using the Loupe browser (10x Genomics,
Inc.), Seurat 5.2.1, and the Signac1.14 package in R software (version 4.4.1) 29,30,37. Quality control was
executed as follows. Clusters enriched for CD3D expression were identified using the Loupe Browser (10x
Genomics) from 'cloupe' files generated by Cell Ranger ARC and subsequently imported into Seurat for
further analysis. Cells with either too few (≤500) or too many (>2,500) expressed genes were excluded to
remove empty or multiple GEMs. Cells with either too few (≤1500) or too many (>10,000) ATAC counts
were also excluded. Cells with a high percentage of mitochondrial genes (≥15%) were excluded to eliminate
dead cells. Cells with a nucleosome signal that was too high (> 2) or a TSS enrichment score that was too
low (≤1) were excluded, as these characteristics are indicative of compromised chromatin structure or
degraded nuclei. Following quality control and normalization, dimensionality reduction was performed
separately for each modality, with principal component analysis (PCA) applied to the RNA data and latent
semantic indexing (LSI) to the ATAC data. Integration of the two modalities was achieved using the
weighted nearest neighbor (WNN) approach, which enables joint clustering and visualization of cellular
states in a unified embedding using the standard Seurat and Signac multiome analysis workflow.
Unsupervised clustering of the integrated data was performed using the 'FindMultiModalNeighbors'
function (reduction.list = list (“pca”, “lsi”), dims.list=list(1:50, 2:50)) and the 'FindClusters' function
(resolution = 1.5). To relate chromatin accessibility to gene expression, gene activity scores were computed
using the 'GeneActivity' function (extend.upstream = 2000, extend.downstream = 0) on the basis of gene
annotations from Ensembl Hsapiens version 98. To visualize chromatin accessibility signals and peak
distributions around specific genes of interest, we generated coverage plots using the 'CoveragePlot'
function implemented in Signac.
Mass cytometry
The monoclonal antibodies used for Helios mass cytometry analysis are listed in Supplementary Table
7. Cell preparation and measurements were performed according to the manufacturer’s instructions for
Helios (Standard BioTools, San Francisco, CA, USA). Briefly, 5.0 × 106 cells were stained with mass
cytometric antibodies. For intracellular staining, samples were prepared using Maxpar Nuclear Antigen
Staining Buffer working solution prior to staining. After being washed twice with Maxpar Cell Staining
Buffer, the samples were fixed with Maxpar Fix and Perm Buffer supplemented with 125 nM iridium
nucleic acid intercalator (Standard BioTools). Following fixation, the cells were washed once with Maxpar
cell-staining buffer, twice with Maxpar water, and resuspended in Maxpar water. Over 200,000 cells per
sample were analyzed using Helios and Cytobank (https://www.cytobank.org) software. The gating strategy
is detailed in Supplementary Fig. 10c.
Associations between T-cell subpopulations
Network analysis was performed to evaluate associations between T-cell subpopulations in the
peripheral blood. Network analysis eliminates false (pseudo)correlations due to confounding effects
between multiple variables. In addition, the modified path consistency (PC) algorithm, a modification of
the original path consistency algorithm, was used to address the redundant data that frequently occur in
biological data 38,39. The PC algorithm requires variable selection when calculating partial correlation
coefficients (associations among three or more variables) of the first order or higher. Therefore, the
estimation is repeated several times to reduce the dependence on variable selection, and edges with a high
frequency of occurrence are selected. In the present analysis, the estimation was repeated 1,000 times, and
edges inferred more than 500 times were chosen as thresholds.
Mice
Female C57BL/6J (B6) mice were purchased from CLEA Japan (Tokyo, Japan, JAX stock no. 000664).
They were maintained in a specific pathogen-free environment and used for experiments at 8–12 weeks of
age. Animals were housed with a 12 h light–dark cycle (lights on at 8:00). The temperature was maintained
at 23 °C (21–25 °C) with a relative humidity of 50% (30–70%). All animal experiments were approved by
the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of Saitama Medical University (Approval No. 4081 and
4191).
Tumor model
MCA 205 is a fibrosarcoma of B6 origin induced by i.m. injection of 3-methylcholanthrene. The tumor
has been maintained in vivo by serial s.c. transplantation in syngeneic mice and was used within the 9th
transplantation generation. Single cell suspensions were prepared from solid tumors by digestion with a
mixture of 1 mg/ml collagenase type Ⅳ, 50 µg/ml DNaseⅠ, and 100 µg/ml hyaluronidase for 2 hours. The
cells were filtered through a 70-μm cell strainer, washed, and suspended in HBSS for inoculations. B16
melanoma were cultured in complete medium (CM) at 37 °C and 5% CO : RPMI, 10% FBS, 1 % Penicillin-
2
Streptomycin, 1 % Non-Essential Amino Acids, 1 mM Sodium Pyruvate, 2 mM L-Alanyl-L-glutamine,
10mM HEPES. Tumor cells were routinely tested for mycoplasma contamination using MycoStrip tests
(InvivoGen).
T cell sorting and culture
Mice were subcutaneously injected in the lateral flank with 1 × 10⁶ B16 or 2 × 10⁶ MCA205 tumor
cells. On days 10 to 12 after tumor inoculation, inguinal lymph nodes were harvested, mechanically
dissociated using a syringe plunger, and passed through a 40 μm cell strainer to prepare single-cell
suspensions. CD4+ T cells were purified using Dynabeads FlowComp Mouse CD4 (Thermo Fisher). For
sorting, cells were stained for 30 min at room temperature with PE-conjugated anti–mouse CD194 (CCR4)
and Brilliant Violet 421–conjugated anti–mouse CD196 (CCR6) monoclonal antibodies (both at a 1:40
dilution), and APC-conjugated anti–mouse CD183 (CXCR3) monoclonal antibody (1:100 dilution)
(BioLegend). Th7R cells were defined as CXCR3±CCR4−CCR6+ CD4+ T cells, and Th1 cells as
CXCR3+CCR4−CCR6− CD4+ T cells and were sorted using a SONY SH800Z cell sorter (Supplementary
Fig. 11a). Sorted Th1 and Th7R cells were stimulated with Dynabeads Mouse T-Activator CD3/CD28
(Thermo Fisher) and cultured in CM supplemented with IL-2 (15 IU/mL). Lymphocytes were cultured for
7–14 days and used for adoptive cell transfer (ACT).
Adoptive T cell transfer and TIL analysis
MCA205 cells (2 × 106) were inoculated subcutaneously along the abdominal midline of B6 mice. One
day before ACT, cyclophosphamide (50 mg/kg) was administered intraperitoneally as a single dose; on the
following day, cultured Th1 or Th7R cells were injected via the tail vein at the indicated cell numbers. No
blinding was performed. Experimental and control mice were housed under identical SPF conditions and
bred separately. Tumor size was measured on 2–3 days per week with calipers in two orthogonal dimensions,
and tumor area (mm²) was calculated as the product of the two perpendicular diameters. For survival
analysis, the endpoint was defined as tumor area exceeding 100 mm2 or upon the appearance of tumor
ulceration. Euthanasia was carried out by cervical dislocation under inhalation anesthesia with isoflurane.
All experiments were conducted in accordance with institutional guidelines, and the maximum allowed
tumor size or tumor burden was not exceeded in any experiment.
For TIL analyses, MCA205 (2 × 106 cells) were inoculated subcutaneously into the left flank of B6
mice. After the same cyclophosphamide preconditioning, ACT was performed, and tumors were harvested
on day 6 post-ACT. Tumor tissues were digested in RPMI containing Liberase TL (25 µg/mL for MCA205;
100 µg/mL for B16) at 37 °C for 30 min with gentle inversion. Cell suspensions were passed through a 40-
µm cell strainer, enriched by 40/80% Percoll density-gradient centrifugation, and used for mass cytometry
analysis (Supplementary Fig. 11b). The monoclonal antibodies used for mass cytometry analysis are listed
in Supplementary Table 7.
Statistical analyses
GraphPad Prism 10 (GraphPad Software, San Diego, CA, USA) was used for statistical analysis. The
data are presented as the means ± standard errors of the means unless otherwise specified. Differences
between two groups were evaluated using Student’s t test. Comparisons across multiple groups were
conducted using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Tukey’s post hoc test. Survival curves were
generated using the Kaplan–Meier method, with differences and hazard ratios assessed using the log-rank
(Mantel‒Cox) test. All P values were two-sided, and values < 0.05 were considered to indicate statistical
significance.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

In this manuscript, Dr. Takei and coworkers provide compelling data of the identification of a specific CD4+T cell population (Th7R) in the tumour microenvironment of lung cancer patients that are postulated to support precursor exhausted CD8+ T cells (Tpex) as good predictors of immunotherapy response. Although overall the results are very interesting and convincing, some major concerns arise during the study of the manuscript that from my point of view need to be addressed before I could recommend the publication of the manuscript.
Major comments:
1.- The origin of the data in the multiple analysis results confusing and need to be better clarified. In section 1 of the results (lines 118-136), a group of sorted Tcells is used to generate signatures to differentiate major CD4+ T cell populations. These signatures are used first to identify Tcell clusters identified in scRNA-seq analysis of 5 patients (lines 83-117). Nevertheless, in the second section of the results (lines 152-175), these signatures are used to further characterize “ three additional TIL and PB scRNA-seq analyses”. The origin of this data is not stated in the manuscript. Are they new patients or public data? Additionally, further in this section (lines 152-175), identified Th7R populations of TME and PB are used to determine differential expression, what data is used for this? , Only the new “three additional studies”? Why is not all the data merged to identify more robust differentially expressed genes?
2.- In the section in where Th7R abundance is associated with treatment response, it is stated that 20 patients have been used. Nevertheless, the characteristics of these patients is not stated. How does response is evaluated in these patients? Have all the patients treated in the same conditions? How many patients are in each response group? Table S8 shows aggregated data on these and don’t offer a lot of information regarding this. Additionally, 20 patients seem a quite small group to determine strong response associated Would it be possible to validate these observations in a larger patient cohort?
3.- In mouse transplant experiments (lines 241-253), purified Th7R cells are injected in mice to evaluate their potential to generate Tpex numbers. Which is the control group here? According to methods, non-injected mice are used as control group. Nevertheless, non-purified CD4+T cells or any other population should be injected in the control group to properly assess and affirm that the excess of Tpex numbers cannot be a general unspecific response to Tcell injection.
Minor comments:
1.- A better methods section is necessary. Number and characteristics of the patients, origins of the data, etc should be clearly stated in the methods section along with the used methodology.
2.- Some figures are highly overcrowded with redundant information. Figures 1 and 2 particularly should be simplified for clarity. In figure 2, an excess of volcano and violin plots with quite redundant information is overwhelming. In both figures, the same UMAP plots are plotted several times with very similar information. I better effort is necessary to reduce the number of graphs for clarity trying to show different layers of information in the same plot.

### Reviewer 2

This study addresses IL-7RhighCCR6+ Th1-like CD4 T cells (termed Th7R) and their association with progenitor exhausted CD8 T cells (Tpex cells )in tumors, peripheral blood and lymph nodes from NSCLC lung tumor patients using scRNAseq/ scTCRseq, and spatial analyses. Additionally, the authors correlate better response to neoadjuvant PD-1 checkpoint blockade in patients with higher Th7R and Tpex. Some findings are also investigated in a non-lung cancer cell mouse model. Th7R cells have been previously identified and characterized in NSCLC patients by the authors and correlated with response rate to immunotherapy (ref 11) even though mostly in PBMCs, but colocalization with DCs/Tpex in triads or TLCs and correlation with PD-1 response rate has been described before by others (refs. 7-8). More importantly, there are several concerns with data shown resulting in lack of support for the conclusions presented in this study.
Major points of criticism:
(1) Data are descriptive and correlative and often lack details to enable reader to understand analysis or data shown. Small patient numbers for single-cell datasets (and even pooled data was analyzed?)
(2) Are the authors proposing that Th7R cells are tumor specific? Do they express PD-1, TOX, CXCL13? But then how to reconcile abundance in blood? Results in this study should be analyzed and appropriately discussed with respect to and in the context of other recent studies on this topic.
(3) Definition of T cell populations is not consistent with studies of other groups and authors do not provide enough evidence to support the proposed annotations.
(4) Markers used to identify key cell types for spatial analysis are insufficient.
(5) The mouse experiment in its current form does not add much value to this study.
Additional Concerns
(1) The introduction is very short and needs to be revised for accuracy.
(2) Initial sentence that Tpex were identified by scRNAseq is incorrect and should be adjusted (original papers had identified those cells in mouse models using flow cytometry based on TCF1/CXCR5 expression, scRNA seq confirmed the unique identify of those cells and their presence in patient tumors). Also, Tpex are a subset of exhausted T cells (NOT effector T cells, cf. line 59) and functionally/phenotypically different from effector T cells.
(3) “Unlike cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs), which lose lack TCF7 expression”
(4) “CD4⁺ T-cell help is essential for inducing effective CD8⁺ T-cell responses, including Tpex 6.” This statement is incorrect, and the cited manuscript does not address this question (Tpex are induced without CD4-help).
(5) “It has been shown that CD4⁺ T-cell-mediated signals, particularly in the presence of antigen-presenting dendritic cells, prevent deep exhaustion of CD8⁺ T cells and promote TCF7 and IL-7 receptor expression 7,8.”, this is also incorrect, CD4⁺ T-cell-mediated signals promote differentiation of Tpex into effector-like cells, not TCF7 and IL7R expression.
(6) References 11 and 13 are duplicates
(7) Even though mentioned in the Method section, giving a brief description of what kind of patient samples (lung cancer cell type, location, prior treatment, gender/age of patients etc) at the beginning of the results section would be appreciated. Alternatively, a summarizing table could be referenced. Overall methods should be more detailed. For example, were TILs cryopreserved before scRNA seq analysis? Were the 5 patients pooled together? Or ran separately or barcoded? Number of cells per patient should be provided and not just the total number of CD4 in PBMC and TILs. If samples were pooled how can TCR sharing be appropriately accessed?
(8) In Fig 1A, “UMAP plots of CD3D+CD4+ cells generated with integrated gene expression data from single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) of peripheral blood (PB) and tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) derived from 5 stage I-II non-small cell lung cancer patients. All 58,687 CD3D+CD4+ cells (50,608 PB-CD3D+CD4+ cells and 8,079 TIL-CD3D+CD4+ cells)”. Are these data from sorted CD3+ CD4+ cells from PBMC and TIL? For TIL scRNA-seq analysis, samples were used after erythrocyte removal.” Therefore, were the CD4 T cells “enriched” based on CD4 mRNA expression detected in 10x? ### Reviewer 3

The topic is highly relevant and challenging in the context of immune-oncology.
The presumed involvement of T CD4 help in the generation and/or maintenance of Tpex is a recent hypothesis emerging from recent articles cited partly by the authors (see Humbling et al Immunity 2025 in press). However, the CD4 partner has not been clearly identified.
This study was conducted in a cohort of NSCLC patients undergoing surgery.
The methodology approach is robust and state-of-the-art including Sc RNAseq, TCR seq, mass cytometry (Hyperion), and multiplex IHC OPAL technology).
The authors have therefore identified both in blood and TME, a new subpopulation called Th7R which is thought to be a "close cousin" of Th1 as the partner of Tpex. These Th7R cells express CXCR3± CCR4- CCR6+, TCF7+ and also characterized by LTB CXCR6, CTLA4, and CXCL13 expression. Th7R are found in TLS where they co-localize with Tpex in the TME and lymph nodes. The presence of Th7R and Tpex in TME was associated with better response to neoadjuvant PD-1 blockade therapy. Furthermore, adoptive transfer of Th7R increased Tpex in a MCA-induced sarcoma in mouse.
The results are robust although they mainly show correlations, and are therefore often descriptive rather than demonstrative.
The article is well written and well discussed.
Here are my main comments
- The presence of this Th7R subset should be validated in other human cancers, at least in a second cancer model (in blood, lymph nodes and TIL if available). In addition, the transcriptomic signature associated with this subpopulation should also be investigated in other cancers using TCGA.
- Th7Rs are found in zone B of TLS. This raises the following question: are Th7R cells different from Tfh? How can the authors differentiate them from Tfh , which also express CXCL13?
- What STATs are expressed by Th7R cells? Given that they are RORC+, one would expect STAT3 to be expressed.
- The mouse model is not really conclusive. This adoptive transfer experiment should be replicated using separately, the 3 sub-populations defined by the authors such as CXCR3+ CCR4- CCR6- (Th1 cells); CXCR3- CCR4+CCR6+ (Th17 cells), and CXCR3± CCR4- CCR6+ Th7R cells. It should also be validated in a second tumor model in mice. For example B16-OVA and OTI/OT II cells if possible. I suggest moving this paragraph on mouse experiments in another section after the data on patients.
Minor points
Lines 186-191: fig. 3A and fig 3B are inversed. Please change in the right sense
lines 244-249: discrepancy between text in the results section, legend of Fig 6A and method; Please make them harmonious.

- The presence of this Th7R subset should be validated in other human cancers, at least in a second
cancer model (in blood, lymph nodes and TIL if available). In addition, the transcriptomic
signature associated with this subpopulation should also be investigated in other cancers using
TCGA.
→In the revised manuscript, initial analysis was performed on 8 early-stage lung cancer patients
who underwent surgery yielding both TILs from lung cancer tissue and peripheral blood (Fig. 1a-
g, Supplementary Fig.1a, b). To demonstrate the robustness of this analysis, additionally we
performed CD4+ T cells using peripheral blood scRNA-seq data from 34 patients, including
locally advanced and advanced lung cancers (Supplementary Fig.3a, b), and peripheral blood
scRNA-seq data from 135 healthy individuals obtained from public data (the Human Cell Atlas
project (https://www.humancellatlas.org/), specifically the Asian Immune Diversity Atlas
(AIDA)) (Fig. 3e, f). Results showed that the SELLlow effector-type cluster group consistently
contained clusters exhibiting Th1, Th17, and Th7R gene expression patterns, achieving good
prediction probabilities and cosine similarity indices using 58 signature genes (Supplementary
Fig.3c, d, g, h). While Th7R was present in healthy individuals, the only CD4+ T cell cluster
significantly decreased after surgical resection of cancer was Th7R (Fig. 8b). Therefore, Th7R
was suggested to be induced by cancer antigens.
As the reviewer suggested, we analyzed data obtained from three renal cell carcinoma (RCC)
patients (Fig. for reviewer 1). Consistent with the analyses of the initial eight stage I–II lung
cancer patients (Fig. 1), the independent cohort of 34 stage III–IV lung cancer patients
(Supplementary Fig. 3a–d), and 135 healthy individuals from public datasets (Supplementary Fig.
3e–h), unsupervised clustering of total CD4⁺ T cells in the RCC samples identified a distinct
cluster exhibiting the Th7R-type 58-gene signature. This cluster was clearly separated from Th1-
and Th17-type clusters and showed high cosine similarity with sorted Th7R cells.
The reason we did not include RCC analysis in the current revised manuscript was that results
from healthy individual data from human cell Atlas-AIDA demonstrated the presence of Th7R
cells even in non-cancerous states, indicating the broader universality. Moreover, the independent
validation using 34 stage III–IV lung cancer patients provided stronger robustness than the small
RCC cohort (n = 3). Nevertheless, we would be pleased to include the RCC analysis results as
additional supplementary material should the reviewers consider it appropriate.
Fig. for reviewer 1
- Th7Rs are found in zone B of TLS. This raises the following question: are Th7R cells different
from Tfh? How can the authors differentiate them from Tfh , which also express CXCL13?
→Thank you for the suggestion. We examined the distribution of BCL6, CXCR5, and IL-21—
transcription factors, chemokine receptors, and cytokines characteristic of Tfh—on the UMAP
derived from TIL scRNA-seq analysis (Fig. for reviewer 2). This revealed cells highly expressing
CXCR5 within the SELLhigh cluster group (in the middle of the UMAP). However, we could not
identify specific clusters highly expressing BCL6 and IL-21 genes. The Th7R cluster (#18+21)
expressed IL-21 to some extent, but its expression was not particularly high compared to other
clusters. For CXCR5 and BCL6, we observed only relatively low gene expression. These results
indicated that typical Tfh cells present in secondary lymph nodes are not found in tumor tissues,
and that Th7R cells do not share properties with Tfh cells beyond CXCL13 expression.
Fig. for the reviewer 2
- What STATs are expressed by Th7R cells? Given that they are RORC+, one would expect STAT3
to be expressed.
→As the reviewer suggested, we re-analyzed the data. STAT3 gene expression was observed in
the Th7R cluster (#18, #21), suggesting higher expression in the TME than in peripheral blood
(Fig. 2a, b, Supplementary Table5). However, no particularly high trend was observed
compared to the Th1 cluster (#13, #26) or the Th17 cluster (#14) (Supplementary Fig.1a, b,
Supplementary Table6). Volcano plot analysis between Th cell types also failed to reveal
significantly different STAT gene expression levels (Fig. 2c, Supplementary Fig.5b). We
speculate that this may be because gene expression does not directly reflect protein levels or
phosphorylation levels.

→As the reviewer suggested, repeated mouse experiments were conducted, and the figures were
revised in Fig. 7a-c. Th7R and Th1 cells isolated by sorting from lymph nodes draining MCA205
skin tumors were i.v. infused into MCA205 skin tumor-bearing mice after ex vivo culture (each
group contains 4 mice). Th7R cells exhibited antitumor therapeutic efficacy comparable to Th1
cells (Fig. 7a), but induced distinct CD8⁺ T-cell phenotypes in the tumor microenvironment (Fig.
7c) (each group contains 4 mice). Th1 transfer increased PD-1⁻GZMB⁺ cytotoxic CD8⁺ T cells,
whereas Th7R transfer resulted in significant increase of PD-1⁺IL-7R⁺ and PD-1⁺TCF7⁺Tpex-
like CD8⁺ T cells. Moreover, Th7R cells derived from melanoma-draining lymph nodes did not
mediate therapeutic effects against MCA205 tumors, demonstratingtumor antigen
specificity(Fig. 7b) (each group contains 5 mice).
